summary:
Mars X Mission is an AI-assisted Mars surface exploration planning system. We developed a single interface that brings NASA planetary data together to help a future Mars astronaut understand the terrain, identify science targets and plan a route. Users choose a region, such as Gale Crater, and layer NASA optical, elevation and thermal data, each shown with its source, date and units. They then mark science targets, build a route with stops and a return to base, and see distance, elevation change, slope and duration. Gemini then writes a mission briefing that explains the plan, its constraints and its data gaps.

The challenge asks for an interface that helps an astronaut understand terrain, find science targets and weigh mobility and environmental constraints. Our system addresses each of these in one workflow, instead of across separate datasets and tools.

It matters because it shifts the question from “where can I walk?” to “where should I explore, what can I learn, and what are the risks?” It also makes public NASA data more understandable and transparent by labeling data limits clearly. It is an educational simulation, not an actual NASA mission.
details:
Mars X Mission is an AI-assisted platform that helps a future Mars astronaut plan a surface expedition. Mars data is usually spread across separate optical, topographic, thermal, spectral and radiation datasets, so the project brings them together in one interface. The user picks a region and sets a base and an objective (our demo uses Gale Crater and Mount Sharp). The system then layers NASA imagery, elevation and thermal data on the map, showing each layer’s source, date, resolution and units. Next, the user marks science targets such as boxwork formations and observation waypoints, and builds a route with science stops that ends back at base. The system calculates distance, elevation change, slope and duration, and flags terrain warnings. Finally, Gemini writes a mission briefing that explains the route, the targets, the assumptions and the data gaps. Our demo, the Boxwork Discovery Expedition, investigates formations that may preserve evidence of ancient groundwater.

The main benefit is that everything sits in one workstation, so users no longer switch between tools to understand terrain, find targets and plan movement. It changes the question from “where can I walk?” to “where should I explore, what can I learn, and what are the risks?” It is also transparent. Every layer shows its source and date, and the system clearly labels data that isn’t available, such as the fact that thermal maps are not live temperatures and radiation data is historical. Future Mars astronauts, mission planners weighing targets against constraints, and educators and learners exploring real NASA data can all benefit from it.

The intended impact is to show how public NASA data can support thinking about future surface missions by making it easier to understand and more open to inspection. It is an educational planning prototype, not a validated safety system and not an actual NASA mission.

We built it with public NASA data and tools: NASA Mars Trek for map layers, tiles and API, ASU Mars Global Data for elevation and thermal data, and Curiosity rover observations for imagery and geology. The AI briefings use the Gemini API. The code is written in TypeScript, with shared typed data structures (MarsLocation, ScienceTarget and MissionAnalysis) that let the modules connect, and the team worked on GitHub with one feature branch per module. The backend has a scientific data service, a route analysis engine and an AI service, and the frontend has a Planetary Explorer map, Terrain and Science panels, a Route Planner and a Mission Dashboard. No special hardware is needed. It runs on ordinary devices.

The project is creative in how it frames the problem. Rather than being another map viewer, it is built around the astronaut’s decision-making, and it builds on the strengths of NASA Mars Trek by adding a unified, astronaut-focused interface on top. It pairs route planning with an AI briefing that explains its own assumptions and limits, and it uses a configurable educational route score (S = wd·D + ws·Sl + wr·R, combining distance, a slope penalty and a roughness penalty). It also treats scientific honesty as a feature, with unavailable data labeled rather than hidden.

As a team, we considered the limits of the data first: thermal data isn’t live and radiation data is historical, so both are shown with their source and date. We considered mobility constraints such as distance, steep areas and equipment, and terrain factors such as elevation, slope and roughness. We planned checks for map loading, layer switching, calculations, AI-failure handling and cross-device use. For feasibility, we used only public NASA data and tools and split the work into six parallel workstreams connected by one shared data contract. We scoped the prototype to real Mars imagery, an interactive map, optical, topographic and thermal data, science markers, route and distance calculations, and Gemini briefings. Future work includes elevation profiles, deeper slope analysis, CRISM mineral data, Curiosity radiation data, 3D terrain and route comparison. Throughout, we labeled it clearly as an educational simulation rather than a real mission.
